passages.t: Gog of the land of Magog
passages.happening:
‘Son of man, set your face against Gog of the land of Magog, the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal’ (verse 2). God will turn him around, put hooks in his jaws and bring him out with his army, together with Persia, Cush and Put, Gomer and Beth-togarmah, and many peoples (verses 4-6).

‘After a long time you will be summoned. In the latter years you will enter a land that has recovered from war’ (verse 8), whose people have been gathered from the nations and live securely. Gog will plan evil: to go up against ‘a land of unwalled villages’ (verse 11), a peaceful people, to seize plunder (verse 12). Sheba, Dedan and the merchants of Tarshish ask whether he has come for spoil (verse 13). ‘You will advance against My people Israel like a cloud covering the land’ (verse 16), so that the nations may know God when he shows himself holy.
passages.hearers:
The oracle is set after a long time, in the latter years, so it looks beyond Ezekiel's own day. Its names come from his world. Magog appears among the sons of Japheth with Gomer, Meshech and Tubal. Meshech and Tubal were peoples of Anatolia known from Assyrian records. Gomer is usually identified with the Cimmerians, who moved into Anatolia from north of the Black Sea. Persia lay to the east, Cush and Put to the south and west. The name Gog has no certain historical referent; many connect it with Gyges, a king of Lydia in the seventh century BC whom Assyrian texts call Gugu, and others treat it as a symbolic name.

The coalition gathers peoples from the far edges of the known world around a small people at its center. Danger in Israel's memory usually came from the north. Unwalled villages would strike an ancient reader: to live without walls was foolish or a sign of complete peace.
passages.later: Magog is named among ‘The sons of Japheth’ (Genesis 10:2). Jeremiah too saw disaster coming from the north (Jeremiah 1:14).
passages.hard:
Who is Gog, and when does this battle take place?

Readers answer in several ways, and this site takes no side. Futurist interpreters, many dispensational premillennialists among them, expect a literal future invasion of the land of Israel by a coalition of nations in the last days; they differ among themselves on its timing. Many other Christian interpreters, most amillennialists and many historic premillennialists among them, read Gog as a symbolic figure for the final gathering of hostile powers against God's people, drawn in the language of ancient enemies and defeated by God. Many scholars read the chapters as early apocalyptic, using the names of distant peoples to picture an ultimate enemy from the edges of the known world. A few have looked for a fulfillment in some past invasion after the exile, though no event fits closely. Jewish tradition has generally expected a war of Gog and Magog before the age of the Messiah. Revelation takes up the names Gog and Magog for the nations gathered at the end (Revelation 20:8).

All these readings agree on the chapter's point: God will defend his restored people and make himself known to the nations. These chapters identify no modern nation, person or event, and they set no date. Attempts to match these names to modern countries by their sound rest on nothing in the text or its ancient geography.
passages.asks: Gog came against a people living in peace, without walls. Ask where you are afraid of being left exposed. And ask what it means that God himself is the defense of his people.

passages.happening: God asks whether Gog is the one he spoke of in former days through his servants the prophets (verse 17). On the day Gog comes against the land, God's fury will rise. There will be a great earthquake in the land of Israel; the fish, birds, beasts and people will tremble; mountains will be overturned and walls fall (verses 18-20). Every man's sword will be against his brother (verse 21). God will judge Gog with plague and bloodshed, torrential rain, hailstones, fire and sulfur (verse 22). ‘I will magnify and sanctify Myself, and will reveal Myself in the sight of many nations. Then they will know that I am the LORD’ (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
The pictures of God's intervention draw on Israel's older stories of God fighting for his people: the plagues of Egypt, the hailstones at Beth-horon, the fire and sulfur on Sodom, and enemy armies that destroyed one another in panic. God fights, and his people do not need to.

Verse 17 suggests that earlier prophets had already spoken of such an enemy, though none of them names Gog.
passages.later: At Beth-horon ‘the LORD cast down on them large hailstones from the sky’ (Joshua 10:11). In Gideon's day the enemy turned their swords on one another (Judges 7:22).
passages.asks: The battle ends with God making himself known. Ask what you are afraid of in the world's future. And ask what it means that the last word belongs to God.
